transcript: A slide fills with words. You stop listening to read, and you fall behind on both. Here's how to spot an overloaded slide and fix it.
When everything is written down, nothing looks important. And in a video, the slide only stays up while the narration runs, so viewers pause or give up.
Try the glance test. Look for three seconds, then look away. Can you say what it was about? Your headline should make a point, not a label.
Keep body text at 24pt or larger. Watch for two ideas fighting on one slide. And if you could read it aloud as your script, move that text.
The words you cut don't disappear. Explanations go into speaker notes, reference detail goes in a handout, and one crowded slide becomes two or three clear ones.
Take a leave policy slide. Before: a label and five dense bullets. After: request leave two weeks ahead, through the HR portal, with three simple steps.
The headline makes the point, the graphic shows the steps, and the narration carries the detail about accrual and reply times.
The slide shows the point; your voice explains it. On Pro, AI directs the video, landing each key point on its word. Start with Basic at powerpoint2vid.com.
